To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the HCR of adenovirus type 5 was normal in fibroblast cultures from patients with xero‐derma pigmentosum, but reduced in fibroblastic cultures from patients with Cockayne's syndrome.

sunlamp‐exposured Ad 2 is not repaired by excision repair deficient xeroderma pig‐mentosum fibroblasts, but is repaired in a normal fashion by fibroblasts derived from patients with Bloom's syndrome, ataxis telan‐giecta‐sia, and Huntington's disease.

the host cell reactivation of adenovirus type 1 (Ad 1) exposed to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from a GE sunlamp was normal for fibroblasts obtained from patients with Bloom's syndrome (BS), ataxia‐telangiectasia (A‐T), and Huntington's disease (HD).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new technique for the analysis of the repair of DNA damaged by ultraviolet light in mammalian cells.
the study of the molecular mechanisms of carcinogenesis.
the development of a novel method for the study of DNA repair processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the sunlamp HCR technique is useful in the study of excision repair deficiency in xeroderma pigmen­tosum, but that it is not useful as a general assay for DNA repair deficiency in other diseases associated with DNA damage sensitivity.
there is no evidence of a DNA repair defect for sunlamp‐induced DNA lesions in these three diseases.
there is no significant difference between normal and DNA repair deficient fibroblast strains with regard to the HCR of adenovirus type 5 after exposure to ultraviolet radiation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HCR of Ad 2 Vag synthesis is not a useful technique to detect DNA repair deficiencies for fibroblasts derived from ataxia telangiectaia, Bloom's syndrome, or Huntington's disease.
sunlamp radiation is a poor inducer of DNA damage in the fibroblasts used in our studies.

the HCR of Ad 2 Vag synthesis after sunlamp exposure is in the normal range when the fibroblasts are derived from patients representing the three diseases associated with DNA excision repair deficiencies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HCR assay for DNA repair in cultured cells is a useful tool in the evaluation of the DNA repair capacity of cells from patients with a variety of genetic diseases.
the HCR of UV damaged Ad 2 is a sensitive and reliable method for the study of DNA repair.
we were able to identify a novel mechanism of resistance to the cytotoxic effects of sunlamp‐irradiated adenovirus in Bloom's syndrome fibroblasts.
